lead_characters.hook: Amir is the exhausted center of the piece: a young defense-tech founder trying to keep a battery/drone startup alive while managing investors, military meetings, roommates, and his own chemically altered drift. He’s smart, status-conscious, and perpetually half-irritated, with the kind of deadpan authority that comes from being the only person in the room who actually understands the machine.
lead_characters.name: Amir
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, South Asian or Middle Eastern-coded, founder/engineer, urban professional
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network — fast, brittle intelligence with social defensiveness and buried panic — but with a more physically lived-in, hangout-world texture. It gives an actor the chance to play competence, contempt, and fatigue in the same beat.

lead_characters.hook: Alexey is the drifting observer inside the lab ecosystem: a bouncer/security worker who reads serious literature, smokes constantly, and keeps trying to turn his life into art without ever fully committing to the form. He’s funny, self-lacerating, and sexually awkward, with a melancholy that makes him feel like the script’s most porous character.
lead_characters.name: Alexey
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, Eastern European-coded, security guard / aspiring filmmaker
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Cera in Funny People or Jesse Plemons in Game Night — a role built on awkward specificity, wounded stillness, and the ability to make passivity feel emotionally charged. It gives an actor room for comic discomfort, vulnerability, and a low-key romantic pull.

lead_characters.hook: Lucia is the sharpest social counterweight in the group: a writer with a pseudonym, a day-job history, and enough self-possession to call out the men around her without losing her own softness. She moves between flirtation, literary ambition, and practical survival, and the script gives her a real sense of interiority through her poetry and rejection scenes.
lead_characters.name: Lucia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s, writer/artist, likely immigrant or diaspora-coded
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Greta Gerwig in Frances Ha or Ayo Edebiri in The Bear — quick intelligence, romantic skepticism, and the ability to make creative frustration feel alive rather than generic. It offers an actor a chance to play wit, longing, and self-protection in equal measure.

lead_characters.hook: Alana is the quieter domestic anchor around Amir’s chaos, but she’s not passive; she tracks the room, manages logistics, and registers the social weather with a sharper eye than she first appears to have. Her scenes suggest a person who is increasingly aware of the cost of being adjacent to someone else’s ambition.
lead_characters.name: Alana
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Beanie Feldstein in Lady Bird or Molly Gordon in Theater Camp — a role that can look light on the page but gives an actor the chance to play contained frustration, warmth, and the emotional labor of being the sane one in the room.

lead_characters.hook: Virgil is the polished fraud inside the startup machine: socially useful, intellectually shallow, and exactly the kind of person who can sell a dream he doesn’t understand. He’s funny because he’s so transparently out of his depth, but he also functions as a real pressure point in Amir’s professional life.
lead_characters.name: Virgil
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Nicholas Braun in Succession — comic entitlement with just enough insecurity underneath to keep the character from becoming a pure punchline. It gives an actor a chance to play charm as a liability.

lead_characters.hook: Mass is the physical, working-class presence in the orbit: a security guy, drinking buddy, and practical hanger-on whose body and habits are always part of the scene. He’s less verbal than the others, but he adds a grounded, masculine counterweight to the more literary and aspirational characters.
lead_characters.name: Mass
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Steven Yeun in early indie ensemble work or Lakeith Stanfield in Sorry to Bother You — a role that can turn minimal dialogue into lived-in presence. It gives an actor room to communicate status and fatigue through behavior.

lead_characters.hook: Michelle is the blunt, no-nonsense pressure valve in the group, the one who says what everyone else is circling. She reads as someone with little patience for posturing, which makes her scenes useful as a reality check inside the ensemble.
lead_characters.name: Michelle
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Janelle Monáe in an ensemble scene or Zoë Kravitz in a sharp supporting turn — concise, cutting, and socially dominant without needing much screen time. It gives an actor a chance to land authority fast.

lead_characters.hook: Noor is one of the meta-theatrical mirrors in the script: an actor reading Alexey’s scene, calling out his behavior, and helping turn the screenplay itself into social material. She’s playful but not indulgent, which makes her feel like a real peer rather than a decorative side character.
lead_characters.name: Noor
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Auli'i Cravalho in an indie ensemble or Rachel Sennott in a self-aware comedy-drama — a role that can pivot between teasing, intimacy, and blunt truth-telling. It gives an actor a chance to be both inside and outside the joke.

lead_characters.hook: Catherine is the other half of the actor-reader pair, and she helps give the script a social world beyond the lab and the couple dynamics. She’s lightly comic, observant, and part of the script’s broader interest in how artists talk when they’re not performing for an audience.
lead_characters.name: Catherine
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Haley Lu Richardson in a conversational indie or Sabrina Impacciatore in a sharp ensemble turn — a role that rewards timing, chemistry, and the ability to make a small scene feel specific. It gives an actor a chance to create texture quickly.

lead_characters.hook: Samir is the ideological conscience in the later material: the person who remembers what the others used to believe and is willing to say the quiet part out loud. He’s less about plot than pressure, but he gives the script a sharper political edge.
lead_characters.name: Samir
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Riz Ahmed in a dialogue-heavy indie or Adam Driver in a politically charged chamber piece — a role where conviction and disappointment are both playable. It gives an actor a chance to sound like someone who has actually thought through the stakes.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The defense startup built around autonomous undersea missiles is a fresh, immediately legible hook, and it sits inside a very specific social world. audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clear millennial/Gen Z hangout-world appeal, but the appeal is narrow and heavily dependent on taste for elliptical, literary, anti-plot material. The defense-tech angle gives it some topical intrigue, yet the page is far more interested in mood and drift than in a broadly legible commercial engine.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Scenes accumulate more than they escalate, and the script repeatedly cuts away before pressure can fully land. The startup stakes, the relationship tensions, and the creative frustrations are all present, but they rarely converge into a forward-driving sequence of cause and effect.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds of deeper material in the startup’s military implications, the characters’ class positions, and the way intimacy and exploitation blur in the lab. creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The combination of defense-tech startup culture, literary self-consciousness, druggy intimacy, and geopolitical chatter is unusual and confidently specific. character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Amir, Alexey, Lucia, Alana, Virgil, and Michelle all have distinct textures, and the social chemistry is real in the lab scenes and apartment scenes. tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakably heightened: earnest grief, blunt profanity, romantic banter, and graphic violence all coexist in the same register. That mix gives the script a distinct soap-horror flavor, even when the scenes sometimes swing hard between comedy, melodrama, and gore.

The final reveal reframes the killings in a way that is easy to follow, though not especially surprising once the revenge logic is in motion.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school, homes, police station, and party spaces all feel like part of the same teen ecosystem, and the script repeatedly returns to the social rules of popularity, gossip, and status. audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and the slasher frame gives it a clear audience lane, especially for teen-horror viewers. The emotional hook is present in the friend-group betrayals and romantic crosscurrents, but the sheer number of characters and repeated relationship turns make the commercial promise feel more diffuse than streamlined.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The body count and escalating attacks keep the story moving, and the reveal structure gives it forward pressure. The middle spends a lot of time on conversation-heavy group scenes and repeated emotional resets, so the drive comes in waves rather than with a constant tightening grip.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in the insecurity, friendship fractures, and the way each character performs identity for the group. The script mostly keeps those ideas on the surface through direct dialogue, so the emotional subtext is visible but not yet fully layered.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a very specific teen voice and leans into messy, overtalkative social dynamics inside a slasher framework. The execution is familiar in its revenge-killer structure, but the volume of interpersonal chaos and the long-form friend-group banter give it a recognizable personality.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sammy, Lucy, Faye, Austin, and Ryan each have strong behavioral signatures, and the script gives them distinct social rhythms. relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The friend group generates a lot of playable combinations, especially Sammy/Lucy, Austin/Lauren, and Faye/Daniel, and those pairings keep the story socially active. considerations.area: The ensemble could be slightly more selective.
considerations.detail: The script has enough characters for a lively friend-group movie, but a next pass could consider which relationships truly need independent screen time versus which ones can be folded into the same social beats. That would protect the momentum while keeping the cast footprint and audience tracking cleaner.

considerations.area: The middle leans hard on conversation.
considerations.detail: Several cafeteria and hangout scenes spend a lot of pages on the group explaining feelings and status changes directly. One lever would be to let a few of those turns land through action, interruption, or a sharper visual beat so the horror pressure keeps building while the relationships still register.

considerations.area: The killer logic is strongest when it stays simple.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps moving and there is always another confrontation, confession, or body count escalation to carry it forward. creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to taboo territory — queer desire, family rejection, and serial violence — and it does so without hesitation. That gives the project a magnetic supporting role for an actress who can play wit, control, and a flicker of surprise in the same scene.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Zara is a standout supernatural foil.

strengths.evidence: Caroline's book about free will and Priya's art-world self-possession, both of which David responds to before the wish is fully understood.
strengths.what_it_means: Caroline and Priya are not just targets of the spell; they each represent a different kind of adult connection, which makes the eventual choice feel earned. That gives the film a stronger emotional aftertaste than a standard fantasy-comedy because the ending is about self-recognition, not just getting the girl.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The romance lands through contrast, not wish fulfillment.

strengths.evidence: Marcus decoding the wish, calling it a 'free trial,' and pushing David toward the right questions.
strengths.what_it_means: The best-friend role functions as the audience surrogate and the pressure-release valve, which keeps the supernatural premise from floating away. That makes the script attractive to actors who specialize in sharp, scene-stealing support and to producers who want a reliable tonal anchor.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Marcus gives the movie its grounded comic spine.

strengths.evidence: The repeated set pieces across the coffee shop, car rental counter, bookstore, gym, office elevator, grocery store, riverside cafe, and art gallery.
strengths.what_it_means: Coffee shops, bookstores, gyms, galleries, and apartment buildings all become repeatable encounter spaces, which gives the film a strong visual rhythm and a low-cost production footprint. That kind of urban texture plays well for buyers looking for a contemporary relationship movie with enough specificity to feel current.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The city is used as a dating machine.

strengths.evidence: David canceling the wish, then calling Caroline and showing up as himself at Renner Street Coffee.
strengths.what_it_means: The final movement turns the supernatural premise into a human choice: David rejects the shortcut and walks toward a real conversation. That gives the film a satisfying close for audiences who want romance with a point of view, not just a gimmick.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending earns its emotional thesis.

considerations.area: The middle section repeats the same wish-beat.
considerations.detail: The montage of women responding to David's new aura is effective as escalation, and a next pass could consider compressing one or two of those encounters so the emotional turn arrives a little sooner. That would protect the momentum while keeping the 'free trial' idea intact.

considerations.area: Caroline becomes the emotional destination late.
considerations.detail: The Caroline thread is the most resonant romantic lane, and the version of the script where her presence is seeded a little earlier could make the final call and coffee-shop reunion land with even more inevitability. The material already points there; this is about foregrounding that destination sooner.

considerations.area: The city footprint is pleasantly broad.
considerations.detail: The script uses a healthy spread of contemporary locations — coffee shop, restaurant, antiquities store, apartment, rental counter, bookstore, gym, office, grocery, gallery, rooftop, and street exteriors. If production wanted to simplify, a few of those encounter spaces could be folded together without changing the story engine.

considerations.area: Zara's rules are clean and playable.
considerations.detail: The wish logic is already easy to follow, and the one place to protect is the distinction between being desired and being remembered. Keeping that distinction crisp in every Zara scene preserves the emotional thesis and makes the ending feel earned.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streaming romantic comedy-drama with a supernatural hook; specialty theatrical for adult audiences
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be greenlit off a strong lead and a compelling Zara without requiring a large ensemble or expensive effects package. The contemporary setting, PG-13 tone, and clean high-concept premise fit the current buyer appetite for dateable, exportable genre-romance with a clear trailer hook.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a romantic fantasy that plays like a character study, not a spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards restraint: the magic is simple, the scenes are conversational, and the payoff comes from behavior rather than effects. That makes it especially attractive to directors who can get chemistry, timing, and tonal control out of small moments instead of leaning on set pieces.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with one or more features, or TV-to-feature filmmakers who already know how to stage intimate dialogue and clean emotional turns. The sweet spot is someone drawn to performance-forward storytelling, urban texture, and lightly magical premises that stay emotionally grounded.

lead_characters.hook: David is a quietly self-conscious single man who has spent so long rehearsing himself that he barely trusts his own instincts. He is funny in a dry, apologetic way, but the real engine is the ache underneath the jokes: he wants to be seen without having to perform for it.
lead_characters.name: David Calloway
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Giamatti in *Sideways* or Jake Gyllenhaal in *Stronger* — a lead whose inner life is the movie, with comedy and self-reckoning living in the same face. Actors who want a role that lets them play awkward charm, romantic longing, and a late-film moral pivot will chase this.

lead_characters.hook: Zara is a genie with the patience of someone who has seen every version of human desire and is no longer impressed by the packaging. She is elegant, amused, and exacting, but the script lets her become something more interesting than a trickster: a witness to the difference between wanting and understanding.
lead_characters.name: Zara
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Tilda Swinton had in *Only Lovers Left Alive* or Cate Blanchett in *Blue Jasmine* — a character whose authority and mystery are the performance. It gives an actress the chance to play command, wit, and a subtle emotional thaw without ever leaving the frame.

lead_characters.hook: Marcus is David's best friend and the only person in the movie who can puncture the fantasy without killing the fun. He is funny, grounded, and smarter than he pretends to be, with the easy authority of someone who knows exactly how ridiculous his friend is and loves him anyway.
lead_characters.name: Marcus Green
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Mahershala Ali in *Moonlight*'s friend/mentor register or Donald Glover in *Atlanta*'s grounded comic mode — a role that gets to be the smartest person in the room without becoming a lecture. Character actors who can do warmth, timing, and lived-in friendship will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Caroline is the version of adult attraction that feels calm, intelligent, and unforced. She reads as self-possessed rather than performative, which makes her the perfect counterweight to David's wish-driven chaos and gives the film its most grounded romantic energy.
lead_characters.name: Caroline Price
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Greta Gerwig had in *Frances Ha* or Michelle Williams in *Take This Waltz* — a woman whose intelligence and stillness are the point, not the decoration. Actresses who want a romantic lead built on specificity, not melodrama, will see the appeal immediately.

lead_characters.hook: Priya is sharp, self-possessed, and unbothered by the room's opinion of her, which makes her feel instantly adult in a story full of projection. She has the kind of clarity that makes David slow down, because she is not asking to be chosen — she is already choosing.
lead_characters.name: Priya Anand
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Ayo Edebiri in *The Bear*'s more self-contained moments or Zoe Kazan in *Ruby Sparks* — a role that lets an actress play intelligence, wit, and romantic authority without overexplaining herself. It is especially attractive to performers who want a modern, grounded female lead with real conversational chemistry.

lead_characters.hook: Miranda is warm, quick, and briefly open in a way that makes David think he might be getting somewhere. She functions as one of the film's early mirrors for the wish, showing how fast charm can feel like destiny before it evaporates.
lead_characters.name: Miranda
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact, memorable romantic-support role that actresses like Allison Janney or Kathryn Hahn can make feel larger than the page. It gives a performer a clean comic-romantic beat and a sharp exit that the audience remembers.

lead_characters.hook: Jessica is the first person to make the wish feel operational in the real world, turning a routine rental counter into a flirtation with consequences. She is efficient, playful, and just bold enough to make David question what changed.
lead_characters.name: Jessica
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing part that lets an actress do instant chemistry in a single exchange, the way supporting players do in *Set It Up* or *Crazy, Stupid, Love*. It is a strong audition-piece role for someone who can land charm fast and leave a mark.

lead_characters.hook: Claire is bookish, self-aware, and a little surprised by her own boldness, which makes her feel like a real person rather than a fantasy beat. She helps widen the movie's romantic texture by showing that the wish works on women with different energies, not just one type.
lead_characters.name: Claire
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that plays like a smart indie-romance supporting turn, similar to the grounded charm of Emily Blunt in *The Young Victoria* or Jenny Slate in *Obvious Child*'s lighter registers. It gives an actress a quick, memorable scene with a clear emotional temperature.

lead_characters.hook: Helen is the neighbor who makes the spell feel socially real, not just flirtatious. She is married, familiar, and suddenly attentive, which gives the wish its most uncomfortable proof that the effect is broader than David can manage.
lead_characters.name: Helen
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of adult-support role that can land with the specificity of Patricia Clarkson in a few scenes — a woman whose brief attention tells a whole story. It gives an actress a chance to play temptation, irony, and everyday realism at once.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends prestige historical drama with sports-page momentum and moments of dark, ugly authoritarian menace. The script knows when to let the match breathe and when to turn the screws, which gives it a distinct and hard-to-mistake identity.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This feels like a story that should exist: a national sports hero whose greatest act is refusing to let his talent be absorbed by fascist theater. The combination of football choreography, propaganda pressure, and personal defiance creates a fresh and memorable dramatic lane.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the opening World Cup sequence and stays legible: Sindelar is a star athlete under fascist pressure, and the match itself becomes the arena for resistance. The script keeps the central question clear all the way to the final whistle.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Vienna in the Anschluss period is rendered with strong institutional and social texture: newsroom, café, Gestapo office, locker room, church, street, and stadium all feel like parts of the same tightening system. The world is not just backdrop; it actively shapes every choice Matthias makes.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, sellable engine: a sports legend forced into a political spectacle, with a built-in underdog payoff and a famous historical figure at the center. The audience is broad for prestige-drama buyers and sports-history viewers, though the period setting and political specificity keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with purpose toward the Anschluss match, and the repeated pressure from Nazis, teammates, and institutions keeps the story active. Some stretches are more atmospheric and explanatory than propulsive, but the match countdown gives the feature a strong spine.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: On the surface this is a resistance sports drama, but beneath that are themes of legacy, complicity, identity, and what history remembers. The repeated parallels between football rules and political rules suggest deeper thematic layers that reward attention.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script makes a sports biopic feel like a political act, and it commits to the idea that a football match can carry historical consequence. The choice to dramatize resistance through play, gesture, and public spectacle gives the material a confident identity.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sindelar is charismatic, principled, and physically expressive, with a strong contradiction between showman and dissenter. Camilla, Walter, Leopold, and Heinrich add meaningful pressure and texture, though the story remains most powerfully anchored to Matthias.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Matthias and Camilla have real romantic charge, Matthias and Heinrich have a strong mentor-athlete bond, and the team dynamics around Hans and Karl create usable friction. The ensemble is functional and story-generating, though the feature still lives primarily through Matthias’s orbit.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige sports drama with a built-in historical climax and a lead role actors will want to fight for. By turning a football match into an act of national defiance, the script gives producers a clean, marketable hook and a finale that lands as both crowd-pleaser and political statement.

strengths.evidence: Matthias is pressured to play the Anschluss Match, then refuses the Nazi jersey and scores in the black Austrian kit while the crowd chants his nation’s name.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives buyers a clean prestige hook with built-in emotional lift: a public hero using the one thing he’s famous for as an act of defiance. It will attract actors who want a role with physical charisma and moral stature, and producers looking for an awards-capable historical lead.
strengths.dimension_or_area: A sports legend becomes the resistance.

strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly returns to the upcoming match, training, locker-room pressure, and the final 90-minute showdown at Praterstadion.
strengths.what_it_means: The story has a built-in countdown and a public arena where every choice becomes visible, which is exactly the kind of structure that keeps a feature moving. Sports buyers, prestige streamers, and theatrical audiences all understand the stakes instantly because the final act is a game with political consequences.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The match is the movie’s climax engine.

strengths.evidence: The newsroom, café, Gestapo headquarters, church, apartment blocks, and stadium all show different faces of the same political takeover.
strengths.what_it_means: The city is not decorative; it becomes an ecosystem of surveillance, propaganda, and social pressure that gives the film a strong period identity. That kind of world texture is attractive to directors who want to stage history through lived-in spaces rather than speeches.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Vienna feels like a tightening trap.

strengths.evidence: He dances, flirts, argues, trains, defies the Nazis, and turns the pitch into a political statement.
strengths.what_it_means: He gets charisma, athleticism, romance, public performance, and quiet moral resistance in one role, which is the kind of part that can reframe an actor’s range. Mid-career leading men with physical presence and prestige ambitions will see this as a showcase vehicle.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Matthias is built for an actor.

strengths.evidence: Camilla challenges his worldview, Heinrich urges him to play, and Hans embodies the seductive pull of collaboration.
strengths.what_it_means: The Matthias-Camilla romance, the Matthias-Heinrich mentorship, and the Matthias-Hans rivalry give the film multiple emotional lanes beyond the central historical event. That helps the project play to adult audiences who want character dynamics, not just a sports outcome.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The supporting relationships carry real charge.

strengths.evidence: The salutes, banners, speeches, newspaper propaganda, and staged match all operate as public spectacle.
strengths.what_it_means: The film’s political material has a cinematic angle because it shows fascism as performance, pageantry, and crowd manipulation rather than abstract history. That makes the material especially appealing to directors and buyers who respond to political drama with visual scale.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The script understands propaganda as theater.

classification.tone: Gritty, defiant, elegiac

considerations.area: The café and apartment threads can be streamlined.
considerations.detail: The story already has a strong spine in Matthias, Camilla, the team, and the Anschluss match, so a next pass could consider folding some of the café-business logistics and repeated domestic beats into fewer scenes. That would protect the emotional throughline while keeping the feature moving with even more force toward the final match.

considerations.area: The political pressure arrives in several waves.
considerations.detail: The script has a lot of effective institutional scenes — newsroom, Gestapo office, café raid, protest arrest, and the apartment search — and the version where a few of those beats are combined could keep the escalation feeling even more relentless. The core idea is already strong; the simplification lever is about preserving momentum, not reducing scope.

considerations.area: The match build could be even more concentrated.
considerations.detail: The training montage, locker-room speech, and pregame locker-room confrontation all work toward the same emotional destination. One direction would be to let one of those beats carry more of the burden so the final 90 minutes arrive with maximum charge and less repetition.

considerations.area: The historical specificity is a selling point.
considerations.detail: Because the script names real people, songs, newspapers, and institutions, the production should plan for a clear clearance pass early. That is a manageable development step for a prestige historical feature, and it protects the film’s authenticity while keeping the package clean.

considerations.area: The crowd and stadium work define the budget lane.
considerations.detail: The football finale, public demonstrations, and period crowd scenes place the film above a microbudget footprint, but still comfortably inside a contained prestige feature range. A producer can protect the budget by keeping the story centered on a limited number of key locations and using the stadium as the one major scale event.

buyer_appeal.lane: Prestige historical drama / awards-friendly streamer lane
buyer_appeal.detail: The project can be packaged around one marquee lead and a strong supporting ensemble, with the stadium finale and period Vienna doing the rest of the selling. The historical-sports hook, recognizable real-world figures, and awards-friendly resistance story fit the current streamer and limited-theatrical appetite for elevated adult drama.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to stage history through bodies, crowds, and one unforgettable public act.
director_appeal.detail: The script gives a director a rare chance to turn a sports sequence into a political climax without losing emotional intimacy. It will attract filmmakers who like precise period texture, crowd orchestration, and actors doing heavy lifting inside a visually legible world.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie or prestige-feature directors with at least one period drama or character-driven historical piece behind them, especially those who care about performance-forward storytelling and political tension. The material rewards directors who can choreograph football as drama, use institutions as pressure-cookers, and let a final act land like a public verdict.

lead_characters.hook: A dazzling, self-possessed striker with showman instincts and a stubborn moral center, Matthias lives through movement, rhythm, and control. He is charming without trying, proud without being pompous, and increasingly unable to separate the game he loves from the regime trying to own it.
lead_characters.name: Matthias Sindelar
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Timothée Chalamet in *A Complete Unknown* or Eddie Redmayne in *The Theory of Everything* — a physically expressive lead whose body, voice, and inner life all have to carry the film. Actors will chase the chance to play charisma under pressure, then land a final-act defiance that feels earned rather than declared.

lead_characters.hook: Camilla is elegant, observant, and sharper than the men around her initially assume. She brings wit, worldly intelligence, and a survivor’s instinct to the story, and she becomes the emotional counterweight that forces Matthias to see the world beyond football.
lead_characters.name: Camilla Castagnola
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the showcase space of Alicia Vikander in *The Danish Girl* or Lily James in *Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again* — a luminous presence who can shift from flirtation to pain to moral clarity in the same scene. Actresses looking for a role that is romantic, stylish, and emotionally consequential will respond to her.

lead_characters.hook: Walter is Matthias’s teammate and moral mirror, a player who understands the stakes but is more openly vulnerable to the political pressure around him. His marriage to Margot gives him a personal reason to fear the future, which makes his choices feel lived-in rather than symbolic.
lead_characters.name: Walter Nausch
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting-lead territory Oscar Isaac had in *A Most Violent Year* — a man trying to keep his dignity while the world narrows around him. Actors who like intimate, pressure-cooker drama will be drawn to the role’s loyalty, fear, and emotional restraint.

lead_characters.hook: Leopold is warm, wounded, and quietly brave, a man trying to preserve decency in a city that is stripping it away in public. His café becomes one of the film’s moral centers, and his grief over his son gives the story a human cost beyond the stadium.
lead_characters.name: Leopold Drill
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Mark Rylance in *Bridge of Spies* — a gentle exterior with immense internal pressure, where every pause carries meaning. Character actors who specialize in humane authority and emotional precision will want this part.

lead_characters.hook: Heinrich is the coach who sees football and politics as inseparable, and he speaks with the weary intelligence of a man who knows the game is bigger than the game. He is pragmatic, loyal, and haunted by what history will erase if nobody names it.
lead_characters.name: Heinrich Retschury
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Brendan Gleeson had in *The Banshees of Inisherin* — a seasoned presence with authority, melancholy, and a worldview that can carry a scene with one line. Veteran actors who want gravitas without stiffness will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Hans is the teammate who has bought into the new order, and he gives the film its most dangerous kind of friction: betrayal that still looks like ambition. He is cocky, politically compromised, and emotionally legible enough that his choices sting.
lead_characters.name: Hans Mock
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally split supporting-lead territory that Tom Burke had in *The Souvenir Part II* — a role where charm and self-deception sit right on top of each other. Actors who like playing seductive antagonism from inside the ensemble will be drawn to him.

lead_characters.hook: Philip is the observer who keeps trying to tell the truth in a newsroom that wants obedience more than reporting. He gives the film a civilian point of view on how propaganda colonizes ordinary institutions.
lead_characters.name: Philip Dibbon
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of newsroom pressure role that Jesse Plemons had in *The Post* — a smart, watchful character whose restraint makes the surrounding machinery feel more dangerous. Actors who excel at contained intelligence and quiet alarm will like the part.

lead_characters.hook: Mosser is the institutional gatekeeper who knows exactly how far he can bend before he breaks. He is polished, cautious, and chilling precisely because he sounds reasonable while enforcing the regime’s limits.
lead_characters.name: Herr Mosser
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that Richard Jenkins had in *The Visitor* — a man whose calm exterior becomes the point of tension. Character actors who can make compromise feel active will be interested.

lead_characters.hook: Schrempf is the film’s most overt instrument of state violence, a predator who uses bureaucracy, humiliation, and sexual menace as one continuous weapon. He is not just cruel; he is methodical, which makes him more frightening.
lead_characters.name: Jurgen Schrempf
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain territory Christoph Waltz had in *Inglourious Basterds* — articulate, theatrical, and terrifying because he enjoys the performance of power. Actors who can weaponize charm and precision will want the role.

lead_characters.hook: Otto is Schrempf’s quieter partner, the one who turns intimidation into procedure. He is less flamboyant than Schrempf, which makes him feel even more institutional and harder to read.
lead_characters.name: Otto
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of cold-enforcer role that Michael Shannon has played in prestige dramas — a contained presence whose stillness makes the room colder. Actors who can project menace with minimal movement will be interested.

lead_characters.hook: Karl is the teammate who still believes in the team as a team, even as politics tries to split everyone into camps. He is competitive, loyal, and useful as a pressure valve for the locker-room tension.
lead_characters.name: Karl Sesta
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble-athlete role that Jovan Adepo had in *Fences* — a supporting part that still gets to register pride, frustration, and camaraderie in a vivid way. Actors who want a strong team dynamic without carrying the whole film will like it.

lead_characters.hook: Margot is Walter’s wife and a quiet measure of what the regime threatens to erase. She is present enough to matter emotionally, and her marriage gives the film a domestic stake inside the larger political one.
lead_characters.name: Margot
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of intimate supporting role that Sarah Snook had in *Pieces of a Woman* — brief but emotionally loaded, with the ability to make a larger world feel personal. Actors who can communicate history through stillness will respond to it.

lead_characters.hook: Michl is a dignified football man being pushed out of the institution he helped build. He carries the sadness of someone who understands the game’s beauty and the state’s cruelty in equal measure.
lead_characters.name: Michl Shwarz
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-scene authority role that Stanley Tucci had in *Spotlight* — brief but resonant, with moral weight and institutional history in every line. Veteran character actors will see the emotional precision in it.

lead_characters.hook: Robert is idealistic, defiant, and willing to pay for his convictions. He gives the story a younger generation’s urgency and makes the political danger feel immediate inside Leopold’s family.
lead_characters.name: Leopold Drill’s son, Robert
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of idealist role that Lucas Hedges had in *Manchester by the Sea* — a young man whose conviction is part courage and part self-destruction. Actors looking for a brief but memorable moral spark will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.hook: Felix is the polished bureaucrat who translates authoritarian pressure into career opportunity. He is smooth, managerial, and chilling because he speaks the language of sport while serving power.
lead_characters.name: Felix Linnemann
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of institutional operator role that David Strathairn had in *Good Night, and Good Luck* — a man whose calm professionalism masks the machinery underneath. Actors who can make compromise feel elegant will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Heinrich is the coach who sees football and politics as inseparable, and he speaks with the weary intelligence of a man who knows the game is bigger than the game. He is pragmatic, loyal, and haunted by what history will erase if nobody names it.
lead_characters.name: Heinrich Retschury
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Brendan Gleeson had in *The Banshees of Inisherin* — a seasoned presence with authority, melancholy, and a worldview that can carry a scene with one line. Veteran actors who want gravitas without stiffness will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Uhrmann is the higher-level bureaucrat who understands exactly when to tighten the screws and when to wait. He is less theatrical than Schrempf, which makes his authority feel colder and more systemic.
lead_characters.name: Max Uhrmann
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of command role that Mark Strong has played in prestige thrillers — controlled, intelligent, and dangerous because he never needs to raise his voice. Actors who can project power through restraint will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Egon is the compromised intermediary who has to deliver bad news while trying to keep his own conscience intact. He’s a useful face of institutional surrender.
lead_characters.name: Egon Ulbrich
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small but telling role that Paul Dano often makes memorable in prestige ensemble work — a character whose discomfort tells you everything about the system. Actors who can play shame and obedience at once will like it.

lead_characters.hook: Andreas is the ordinary working man who keeps showing up inside a collapsing world. He brings a little comic friction and a lot of everyday texture to Matthias’s apartment life.
lead_characters.name: Andreas
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of lived-in supporting role that Brian d’Arcy James has in ensemble dramas — practical, specific, and quietly memorable. Character actors who can make a small role feel real will be interested.

lead_characters.hook: Ilana is part of Camilla’s social world and functions as both confidante and warning system. She gives the film a peer-level female perspective on escape, survival, and what people choose to ignore.
lead_characters.name: Ilana
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp ensemble role that Zoey Deutch has played in period and contemporary dramas — quick, socially aware, and able to land a scene in a few lines. Actors who like stylish supporting work will respond to it.

lead_characters.hook: Isabella is another voice in Camilla’s orbit, helping build the social texture of Vienna’s fashion world under pressure. She gives the film a lighter, more observational register without losing the period tension.

lead_characters.hook: Jesse is a laid-off Manhattan data analyst with a wounded ego, a performer’s instinct, and a self-destructive streak he keeps trying to monetize. He is funny, needy, vain, and strangely articulate about his own collapse, which makes him both contemptible and magnetic in the same breath.
lead_characters.name: JESSE PETERSON

lead_characters.hook: Mikey is Jesse's best friend and the story's moral ballast, but he is not passive; he is practical, jealous, funny, and increasingly implicated in the scheme. He reads like the guy who can still pretend this is all a joke until the money and the relationship both become real.
lead_characters.name: MIKEY

lead_characters.hook: Andrea is Mikey's girlfriend and the sharpest strategist in the room, with an MBA brain, a social climber's eye, and a willingness to treat catastrophe like a spreadsheet. lead_characters.name: ANDREA
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the cool intelligence of Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl with the transactional edge of Sarah Snook in Succession. It offers a performance lane where calculation, desire, and moral compromise all stay visible at once.

lead_characters.hook: Brenda is ShareStop's COO: polished, ruthless, and always one step ahead of the room until the room turns on her. She has executive calm, a hard-edged survival instinct, and just enough humanity to make her feel like she could either save the company or bury it.
lead_characters.name: BRENDA MCMCAHON
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the corporate power-player territory of Sarah Paulson in Carol or Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects, where the actor gets to play authority, restraint, and private panic under a perfect surface. lead_characters.hook: Devin is the CEO who wants to sound like a philosopher while behaving like a panicked operator, and that contradiction is the joke and the tragedy. He is vain, performative, and deeply dependent on the machinery he claims to understand.

lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play prestige-corporate absurdity in the vein of Jeremy Strong in Succession, but with more overt comic humiliation. It gives a performer a chance to make executive self-mythology feel both ridiculous and dangerous.

lead_characters.hook: Mario is the script's grand theorist: a billionaire AI figure who speaks in moral philosophy, controls the room through intellect, and treats catastrophe as an experiment. He is elegant, eerie, and convinced that history is something he can model.
